extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and epistemology (readers of Mill and Spencer)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing the validity and warrant of deductive and inductive reasoning, especially the test of inconceivableness versus appeal to uniform experience. Focuses on when reductio, axioms, and experiential grounds justify belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reductio ad absurdum
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of propositions may be shown false by assuming premises and deducing an absurdity; this method (reductio ad absurdum) is allowable to demonstrate the falsity of an assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains form: assume A is mark of B, B of C, C of D; if that leads to contradiction (e.g. A becomes a mark of its own absence), conclude the assumption is false. Notes reductio may be used knowingly to expose falsity; shows how it forces denial of at least one premise when conclusion denied. Example supplied; scoring: valid when contradiction is genuine and traceable to the assumed premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental maxim of ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratiocination rests on the axiom that 'whatever has a mark, has what it is a mark of' (or, for universals, that whatever is a mark of anything is a mark of whatever that thing is a mark of).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim is the assumed ground of syllogistic inference; when someone admits premises but refuses conclusion they violate this axiom. Use this as the explicit assumption underlying deductions and check whether premises and conclusions invoke it consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivableness of the negation as a test of truth (Spencer's doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that 'the inconceivableness of its negation is the test by which we ascertain whether a given belief invariably exists' — i.e., inability to conceive a proposition false is the ultimate warrant for its truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill summarizes Spencer's two-step argument: (1) strongest ground is that a belief 'invariably exists'; (2) inability to conceive its negation shows invariability. Guidance notes that this is Spencer's positive and negative argument, with examples (belief in matter, space, time). Also includes Spencer's canon that the 'most certain conclusion' involves the postulate the fewest times. Critiques and limits are discussed: the test can be fallible and may rest on mistaken associations or tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to uniformity of past experience as the proper evidential ground
rubrics_metrics.description: If a belief is supported by 'the perfect agreement of all pre-existing experience', uniformity of experience is the substantial evidence for the belief rather than inconceivableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues one should state that 'all past experience is in favour' and rest belief on that ground, then evaluate how strong that uniformity is (examples: metals sink vs. swans are white). Guidance: evaluate the pervasiveness and generality of the experience; avoid substituting the incidental consequence (inconceivableness) for direct appeal to experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish inconceivability-as-conception from inconceivability-as-belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Two meanings of 'inconceivable' — (a) inability to form or get rid of an idea (imaginability), and (b) inability to form or get rid of a belief (believability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit which sense is intended when applying the test. Examples: antipodes were imaginable (idea) but unbelievable (belief); 'end to extension' is unimaginable (idea). Many of Spencer's arguments conflated these senses; proper evaluation must keep them separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit inconceivableness-test to simple immediate propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The inconceivableness test is legitimately applicable only to 'simple propositions, the subject and predicate of which are in direct relation' and not to complex propositions requiring mediate proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill cites that complex truths (e.g., Pythagorean theorem) cannot be known by immediate inconceivableness and require mediating proofs. When assessing claims, check whether the proposition is simple/primitive (suitable for the test) or complex (unsuitable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware tradition, familiarity, and association producing apparent inconceivableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconceivableness often arises from tradition, habitual association, or familiarity with one mode of explanation rather than from genuine uniform experience, and so can mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cartesians' inability to conceive action at a distance was due to association with contact mechanics, not lack of experience. Criterion: probe whether inconceivableness stems from historical/traditional associations rather than objective uniformity of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct inspection of experience over substitutional tests
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inability to conceive a negation is credited because it reflects uniform experience, then one should examine the experience itself rather than the secondary test of inconceivableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues it is unnecessary and potentially misleading to substitute a conceivability-test for explicit consideration of the relevant experiences. Practical guidance: state the experiential record, assess its scope and strength (are the facts universal, general, occasional?), and use that to weigh the belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for fallibility of any test including inconceivableness
rubrics_metrics.description: All tests, including inconceivableness, are liable to yield untrue results either from incapacity or carelessness; occasional failure does not justify elevating a fallible test to universal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical counterexamples where formerly 'inconceivable' negatives were later found true (sunrise/sunset belief, antipodes, action at a distance) to assess reliability. Scoring: downgrade confidence if evidence shows prior failures or plausible alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The postulate-count heuristic (Spencer's canon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's rule: 'the most certain conclusion is that which involves the postulate the fewest times' — i.e., prefer lines of reasoning that invoke the universal postulate (inconceivableness) fewer times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill critiques this: repetition of the same assumption across steps does not multiply independent chances of error unless new premises are introduced. When applying this heuristic, check whether repeated invocations introduce independent risks or are the same single axiom restated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize immediate self-evident truths as different
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain beliefs about one's own sensations and states of consciousness (e.g., 'I feel cold', 'I exist') are known per se and their negations are genuinely unbelievable; inconceivableness is appropriate here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat first-person present sensations as examples where belief is immediate and the inconceivableness test aligns with direct knowledge. Distinguish these from beliefs about external reality which require separate evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test by attempting to 'believe' the negation rather than merely imagine it
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply the inconceivableness test correctly, one should attempt to 'believe' the negation (test believability), not merely to imagine or conceive it in idea-form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill stresses that Spencer's proper sense of 'inconceivable' aims at belief; evaluators should explicitly try to accept the negation as true (not just picture it) and note whether it is actually believable in that sense. This avoids conflating imagination with conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using inconceivableness as a proxy for inaccessible experiential checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's defense that one cannot recall or enumerate all experiences (so must use inconceivableness) is inadequate; one need not think of every instance to appeal to experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill counters that general, widespread experience and unanimous testimony can suffice; evaluators should not accept inability-to-enumerate as excuse for reliance on conceivability-tests. When assessing evidence, consider representative scope and unanimity rather than literal enumeration.
